title: Property and Other Assets
objective: After this level you can describe property, commodities and the other things people invest in.
summary: Investments pay through income, a price change or both. Property earns rent and changes in value; commodities trade through futures, as at Osaka's Dojima rice market; gold pays no income.

cards.headline: In 1730, Osaka's rice traders were licensed to trade rice for the future.
cards.body: In Edo-period Japan, rice collected as tax was sold to brokers for rice bills, notes you could swap for rice, and those bills were traded busily. In 1730 the shogunate authorized the Dojima Rice Exchange, with a futures market in rice. Stocks and bonds aren't the only things people invest in.

cards.headline: Two ways anything can pay
cards.body: An investment is anything you acquire to make a gain through income or a rise in value. So ask any asset two questions. Does it pay income along the way? Stocks may pay dividends; bonds pay interest. And will its price change? Total return is the income plus the price gain, or minus the loss. Those two questions sort almost everything.

cards.headline: Property: rent and price
cards.body: Property can pay both ways: buildings can produce rent, and their value can rise or fall. Buying a whole building is a big step, so there's another route. A real estate investment trust, or REIT, is a company that owns income-producing property like offices, apartments and warehouses, letting investors share the income. Some REITs trade on stock exchanges; others are illiquid and hard to sell quickly.

cards.headline: Commodities: price, and only price
cards.body: Commodities include metals, grains and other foods. Level 3's salt was one. Many now trade through futures contracts, agreements to buy or sell a set amount at a set price on a future date, just as Dojima traded rice. Some pay no income at all: gold earns no dividends or interest, so its return depends on someone paying more later. US regulators warn that precious metals are highly volatile.

cards.headline: Other assets: sorted
learned: Returns come from income, price change or both
Property earns rent and changes in value
REITs share property income; some are hard to sell
Commodities trade in futures; gold pays no income

options.label: A share in a company that sells commodities
options.rationale: That's a stock, not a futures contract.

options.label: A loan repaid in grain instead of money
options.rationale: It is an agreement about a future trade.

options.label: An insurance policy on a harvest
options.rationale: It fixes a trade, not an insurance payout.

options.label: A deal to trade a set amount at a set price later

questions.explanation: A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell a set quantity at a set price on a future date.

questions.prompt: A flat earns rent for years and then sells for more than it cost. What is its total return?

options.label: The rent plus the price gain
Just the price gain on sale
Nothing until the flat is sold
options.rationale: Income along the way is part of the return.

questions.explanation: Total return adds the income an asset pays to its change in price.

questions.prompt: Unlike Level 33's shares, which way can gold never pay you?

options.label: Through a rise in its price
options.rationale: Gold can rise in price; that's its only way to pay.

options.label: By being sold to someone else
options.rationale: Gold can be sold; its return depends on the sale price.

options.label: By being traded through futures
options.rationale: Metals do trade through futures contracts.

questions.explanation: Shares can pay dividends and rise in price. Gold pays no dividends or interest, so price is its only source of return.
